summary: Multiflora rose is a fast-growing shrub that can reach 10 to 15 feet tall and form dense, thorny thickets that crowd out native plants. It invades open woods, forest edges, fields, fence lines, roadsides and the edges of marshes. You can tell it apart from other roses by the pair of fringed bracts (stipules) at the base of each leaf stalk, and its stems usually have many curved thorns. A single large plant can produce thousands of seeds that stay alive in the soil for up to 20 years.
history: Multiflora rose is native to eastern China, Japan and Korea. It was brought to the United States from Japan in 1866 as a rootstock for garden roses. In the 1930s the U.S. Soil Conservation Service promoted it for erosion control and as "living fences" to hold in livestock, and it was also planted for wildlife cover and later in highway medians. It then became a problem in pastures and fields and is now found in 41 states.
seasons: Multiflora rose blooms in late May or June with clusters of fragrant white to pale-pink flowers. Small fruits (hips) form over the summer and turn red by mid-September. The hips stay on the plant through the winter.

handling.text: The stems usually have many curved thorns. Small seedlings can be pulled by hand, and smaller plants can be dug out, but all the roots must be removed because they can resprout. Cutting or mowing three to six times per growing season for two to four years can kill it. Because its seeds last for years in the soil, follow-up treatments are likely to be needed. In New York City parks like Kissena, cutting, killing or removing plants without permission from NYC Parks is against park rules, so report it instead.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks like Kissena Park, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
